en: Preface to the *Treatise on the Profound Original Text of the Great Fundamental Ground*. It establishes the five stages of the Vajra.

Because the karmic fruits of sentient beings have continued in succession for immeasurable kalpas, they cannot be entirely eliminated except through the merit of cultivation and realization over three asaṃkhyeya-kalpas; therefore, no shortcuts are established.

The stage of gradual progression: because sentient beings, through a single moment of mental correspondence, are identical to all Buddhas, the stage of the ultimate *dhāraṇī* without remainder is established.
Because the minds of sentient beings contain the *dharmadhātu*, universally fusing it inexhaustibly, the stage of pervasive, perfect, and vast greatness is established.
Because sentient beings, in every thought-moment, adhere to existence and thus oppose the gate of liberation, [the stage of] all... is established.

The state where all phenomena are neither [existent nor non-existent] is established because sentient beings abandon existence and cling to emptiness, thereby falling into the view of annihilationism.
Thus, the position that all phenomena are both [existent and non-existent] is set forth. These five preceding positions constitute the general framework of the Buddha-dharma;

they completely encompass all dharma-gates for destroying hindrances and fully include all dharma-gates that accord with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*), leaving not even the slightest detail out. If one clarifies this meaning, then...
Whether discussing the essence (zong) or the teachings (jiao), or speaking of existence or emptiness, none of these are mutually obstructive.

How could there be the fault of dividing a river to drink its waters and engaging in mutual disputes over right and wrong? Alas, for over a thousand years no one has raised these themes, causing this unsurpassed, wondrous Dharma to remain secret and unproclaimed.
I truly do not understand the reason for this. Perhaps it is because the names and meanings within the treatises are so profound and subtle.
These are all the characteristics of the practice of the Mahāsattvas of the Dharmakāya; they are not within the knowledge of ordinary beings.
Because the Master found it difficult to respond to inquiries, he did not show this treatise to others. Nevertheless, he knows them all and will certainly attain the fruit of Buddhahood.

From the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) downward, he may explain these matters according to his capacity without harming his reputation for virtue. This accords with what the Confucian school calls "knowing what one knows and not knowing what one does not know."

This is to say that what is not known is itself knowledge. I have humbly appropriated this principle and added brief annotations. Regarding matters I do not understand, I shall certainly not force an interpretation;

it is my hope that future students may thereby gain a glimpse of clarity. Should there be those of sharp faculties and superior intelligence who might suddenly enter the profound realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*) and attain thorough penetration, that is what I aspire for.
As for those passages where the meaning and phrasing are already clear, I have likewise not provided further commentary.
Commentary: Readers may understand this for themselves.

The fortieth section, "The Great Determination on Encouraging Retention, Circulation, and the Arising of the Ocean of Great Vows," was made into twenty fascicles in the ancient Korean canon, which corresponds with the preface to the *Awakening of Faith*.
It was not included in either the Song or Yuan canons. In the Ming canon, it was made into eight fascicles, and subsequently combined into four; we now follow this version.

This treatise exhausts the subtle and reaches the ultimate in its wondrousness. It is specifically intended for those of sharp faculties and superior intelligence, while simultaneously serving as a potent cause for the One Vehicle for those of ordinary or limited capacity who follow gradual and expedient teachings.
I pray that all who see or hear it shall cultivate and perfume their minds until seeds are formed;
through long-term maturation, the light of the mind will be manifested, enabling them to immediately enter the stage of Vajra-faith and practice with perfect completeness.
The five stages are manifested simultaneously, in accord with the great vows of the Master and the sincere heart of the Commentator.
Their radiance intermingles and interlaces like a net of precious threads, providing successive guidance that knows no end.

The "Great Fundamental Ground" (*Mahābhūmika*) is the general outline of all dharma-gates. Just as the earth gives rise to the myriad things, its principles and meanings are profound and subtle; thus it is called the "Mysterious Text. Since the thousands of branches and ten-thousand leaves are distributed from it, it is named the "Root. This is a treatise (*śāstra*).

This is the definitive analysis (*viniścaya*). It investigates and explains, serving as an auxiliary to the Buddha’s sūtras. Furthermore, beyond this root treatise, there ought to be a commentary (*bhāṣya*) to further elaborate upon its meaning; it is regrettable that such has not been transmitted.
**The First Section of the Great Decisive Analysis on Taking Refuge in the Boundless Source of Virtue:

Homage to All Luminosity Without Exception** I pay homage to that which is neither one nor many, beyond all rules and stages, incalculable, inconceivable, immeasurable, and singular; together with all the various classes of beings in the realms of existence.
The Chapter on the Fundamental Incalculable Severance of Life: Equal to every atom, there is no dharma; it is also ineffable and non-existent.
It penetrates both being and non-being—this is the discourse on all such dharmas. The Commentary states:

Regarding these two lines of verse (in the Indian śloka meter, where a line consists of eight syllables and four lines constitute one verse; in the palm-leaf Sanskrit manuscript, thirty-two characters are written horizontally), [the meaning is as follows:]...

Each line is translated into Chinese characters, consisting of an unequal number of five or seven syllables, and likewise consists of four lines per verse. There are eight gates. What are these eight?
First, the gate that reveals the central sovereign of the center-within-the-center; second, the gate that reveals the rules and regulations of the path;
third, the gate that reveals the separation from the mixed and the unification; fourth, the gate that reveals the infinite sentient beings; fifth, the gate that reveals the various...
The gate of departing from consciousness; sixth, the gate of revealing that which exists conventionally but lacks substantial reality;

seventh, the gate of revealing the non-existence of objective phenomena; eighth, the gate of revealing the fulfillment of unimpededness. These are called the eight [gates]. Whether within the sphere accessible to thought or beyond it, there is nothing that is not a locus of refuge.

Thus, the one who takes refuge and the object of refuge merge into one. The ten realms of the environment and its inhabitants all enter one’s own mind. This treatise encompasses all the Buddha-dharma of the ten directions and the three periods of time, leaving nothing deficient or remaining. What more could be produced hereafter?
How fortunate that one is able to obtain this wondrous scripture! Within the gate of revealing the principal masters of the middle-of-the-middle [teachings], there are five kinds [of Buddha-jewels].

What are these five? First, the responding-body (nirmāṇakāya) principal master who accords with and follows along; second, the transformation-body (nirmāṇakāya) principal master who is unimpeded regarding existence and non-existence;

third, the dharma-body (dharmakāya) principal master who is the fundamental essence and original nature; fourth, the principal master of the perfected path where both origin and end are utterly transcended; [and fifth, the principal master of the ultimate fruit].
The Lord. Fifth is the Lord of Spontaneous Unimpededness according to Response. These are called the five [bodies]. (The above expands the three bodies into five:

first is the birth-body (*janma-kāya*); second is the transformation-body (*nirmāṇa-kāya*); these two are the response-bodies (*nirmāṇa-kāya*). Third is the dharma-body (*dharma-kāya*); fourth is the self-enjoyment body (*svasaṃbhoga-kāya*); fifth is the other-enjoyment body (*parasambhoga-kāya*); these two are the reward-bodies [*vipāka-kāya*]. [This is the first citation from a sutra in the following text].)
In the *Mahādhāraṇī-sūtra on the Cultivation and Accumulation of the Causes of Practice*, it is said as follows:

At that time, the Devaputra Flower-Wreath Jewel-Light-Clarity addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, how many categories of the First Guide are there—those that are conceivable and those that are inconceivable?
We pray that the World-Honored One will reveal and explain this for us, for the sake of our assembly."
"Great assembly, if you hear his name, constantly recite it and constantly keep it in mind, you shall emerge from the storehouse of ignorance and reach the city of Nirvāṇa.

Thereupon, the World-Honored One addressed the devaputra, saying: "If I were to use my power of supernatural penetrations to proclaim his name for immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) kalpas, I could never finish; I shall now speak of it briefly for the sake of you, the assembly, and proclaim it for you."
It is essential, son of good family. Those who are awakened are numerous, vast, and perfect, exceeding the sands of the Ganges River. Briefly stated, there are five kinds. What are these five?
First, the Buddha as the conforming essence; second, the Buddha as the transformative essence; third, the Buddha as the dharma-essence; fourth, the Buddha of unfathomable depth;
and fifth, the Buddha of responsive manifestation. This is taught extensively, as in the verse: "I prostrate to all..."
Because there is no further illumination [beyond this]. For what reason are all the Guides called "Lords"? It is for three reasons. What are these three?
First, the sense of sovereignty, because they are Kings of the Dharma (the Buddha is the King of the Dharma, possessing mastery over all phenomena).

Second, the sense of being the summit, because he alone is the one in the triple world (above the heavens and below the heavens, only the Buddha is uniquely honored). Third, the sense of pervasiveness, because there is nowhere he does not reach.
(Vairocana pervades all places). This is called the third. Thus has been explained the gate that reveals the central sovereign of the middle-of-the-middle.
Next, the gate that reveals the rules for the path shall be explained (the Jewel of Dharma). Within this gate, there are six kinds. What are the six?
First, the rule of unimpeded mastery in guiding through the resonance of the navel of speech. Second, the fundamental ground upon which one relies.
1. The principle of being of one kind in equality and free from all delusions; 2. The principle of growth and development through adornment, wherein each possesses power; 3.
The principle of ultimate perfection that exhaustively encompasses all without remainder; 4.

The principle of being neither name nor mark, neither essence nor function, and characterized by non-creation and non-action; 5. The principle of spontaneous manifestation, eternally abiding and unchanging.
The ultimate, pure, and perfected rule of non-conceptualization is called the sixth [stage]. (Regarding the five fundamental positions taught in the third section:

by taking the first and second dharmas herein as the third stage of pervasive, perfect, and vast realization; the third dharma as the first stage of gradual progression without transgression; the fourth dharma as the second stage of exhaustive, ultimate retention;

the fifth dharma as the fourth stage where all phenomena are neither [existent nor non-existent]; and the sixth dharma as the fifth stage where all phenomena are both [existent and non-existent]. One should understand the opening and closing of these six and those five. [This concludes the second citation from the Sūtra.]
In the *Vajrasamādhy-asaṅga-vimokṣa-mūla-jñāna-tattva-sūtra*, it is stated as follows:
"Furthermore, Mañjuśrī, if I were to explain them in detail, there are a total of one billion, seventy-three thousand, three hundred and fifty dharma-gates;
these are the rules for the paths upon which the practitioner treads. If I were to explain them briefly, there are a total of six types of practitioners."
The principles of practice and conduct: these six principles comprehensively encompass the ocean-like treasury of all immeasurable and boundless rules.
What are the six? First, the principle of exposition; second, the principle of equality; third, the principle of lineage; fourth, the principle of supremacy.
Fifth is the non-principle; sixth is the eternal principle. This is explained at length, as in the verse: "Neither one nor many, because it is the ground of all principles.
For what reason are all the treasuries of the Dharma called *vinaya* (rules/standards)?
It is for three reasons. What are these three? First is the meaning of a gold mold: while human affairs are easily subject to change, the seal of the Dharma-gate is eternally constant and unchanging.

First is the sense of being a distinct category, because it is like that [district]. Second is the sense of guidance, because it leads the practitioner toward the path of remedy, just as a guide does.
Third is the sense of maintenance, because it skillfully maintains its own specific characteristics without loss or destruction, just as a container holds [its contents]. These are the three.
Thus has been explained the section on the gateway of the rules for the path. Next, the section on the gateway of distinguishing from confusion shall be explained.
The Gate of Unification (the Sangha Jewel). Within this gate, there are three types. What are these three? First is unification through bondage:
the various classes of immeasurable, boundless ignorance and afflictions that lead to rebirth.
Although there is no internal unification, there is external unification, because they establish the meaning of "agreement" through numerical equality and so forth (the ordinary Sangha). Second...

Liberation is unified. Because all the infinite and boundless noble ones of the three vehicles possess the meaning of unification through internal principle and the meaning of unification with external phenomena, (the noble Sangha of the three vehicles) is fully endowed with the state that is neither [one] nor [many].
All the infinite and boundless great assemblies of noble beings within the Vajra-intermediate realm are fully capable of...
Because of the two meanings of "the seal" and "that which is sealed," [there is] the "Holy Sangha of the One Vehicle. This is called the third [point] (citing the scripture, third).
In the *Mañjuśrī-paripṛcchā-sūtra*, the foremost among treatises on meaning, which is infinite and inexhaustible, it is said as follows:
"Although the ocean of the Saṅgha is immeasurable, its fundamental essence consists of only three types. What are these three? First, that which is rootless and..."
The ground of contention; second, the ground of non-contention where both roots are absent; third, the ground of non-contention where roots are present—and so forth, as explained at length.
As the verse says: "Not counting, not conceptualizing, because the immeasurable is one. For what reason are all monastic communities (saṃgha) called "unified" (ekībhūta)?
Because there are two meanings. What are these two? First, the meaning of accumulation; that is, the gathering together of the immeasurable.
Because all infinite distractions and defilements are unified within the body (1). Second is the single meaning:

because all immeasurable and infinite waves of consciousness are stilled and settled within the mind (2). These are called the two. Thus has been explained the gateway of manifesting the unification that is free from confusion.
Next, the gateway of manifesting the infinite hair-pores (sentient beings) shall be explained. Within this gateway, then:
There are three gates. What are the three? First, the gate of the infinite arising of hair-like categories; second, the gate of the infinite arising of hair-like categories of emptiness;
third, the gate of the infinite arising of hair-like categories of resemblance. These are called the three. Within the first gate, there are four types.
What are the four? First, birth from an egg; second, birth from a womb; third, [birth from moisture]; fourth, [birth by transformation].
Moisture-born; fourth, transformation-born. These are called the four. Such four modes of birth encompass the fundamental categories of all immeasurable classes of beings.
Within these, there are three types. What are the three? First, those of the empty class hidden within light;
second, those of the empty class hidden within dark matter; third, those hidden within wind and clouds.

The category of emptiness (*śūnya*). This is called the third [of the internal abiding]. These three categories are empty, and thus not non-empty (the body is like space, not a dull or insentient void).

They are empty because they are hidden (hidden and not manifest, therefore called empty). One should carefully examine that the retinue of the category of emptiness is numerous, yet does not exceed this measure.
Within the subsequent section, there are also three kinds. What are the three? First:
First, the category of semblances that lack logical consistency despite having various appearances, such as illusory transformations and incantations.

Second, the category of semblances that lack logical consistency despite having various appearances, such as transformed medicines and prohibitions (these two preceding categories, though possessing various appearances, do not accord with reason; therefore, they are called "semblances").

Third, the category of semblances that appear according to their source, namely images manifested by one's own deluded thoughts (though these images manifest before one, they are not truly existent; they are also called "semblances"). this is as explained in the four fundamental [treatises]. Second, if this emptiness did not express that [nature], then it would be a mere void.

it is both structured and substantial. Were it not for this stage, all Buddha-dharma would have no place to be established; therefore, it stands at the head of the five stages. The Gate of Fulfilling the Vast and Great. Next, the Gate of the Universal Non-Being of All Dharmas shall be explained. What are its characteristics? The verse says:

Once the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is perceived, then everywhere is entirely the Real, and there are no forms of defiled illusion.)

Chapter Four: The Great Determination of the King of Mountains of the Vajra Jewel Wheel (*Vajraratnacakra-parvatarāja-mahā-viniścaya*). (This section is called the "Jewel Wheel" because it describes various modes of differentiation and transformation;

The commentary states: What meaning is clarified by this verse? It is intended to manifest the great vajra-power of a single body.

Within the essence of the Jewel-Wheel Mountain King, all phenomena proceed through these five stages in succession, gradually evolving until they reach the ultimate state of non-remainder, which is universally pervasive and perfectly complete.

These five positions—namely, simultaneous evolution, sequential evolution, coexistent evolution, and neither-coexistent-nor-non-coexistent evolution—likewise involve simultaneous evolution, evolution at different times, evolution in a single location, and evolution in different locations; they are fully endowed with all these modes.
Complete. Sovereign, sovereign. Because there is no obstruction, [the characteristics of the differentiated modes of turning are briefly explained as being of eight kinds].

If one clarifies this meaning, then one will know that among the great beings who propagated the Dharma throughout past and present, regarding the five stages of the Dharma, there were those who exclusively upheld a single gate—such as the Chan masters of the Five Houses descending from Nanyue and Qingyuan; these are cases of turning [the Dharma] at different times and in different places.

The Grounds and Paths of Practice. The fundamental self-nature of the inexhaustible treasury, the treasury that is the basis for the arising and growth [of all things], and so forth, as explained at length.
Chapter Five: The Great Determination of the Path of the Golden Wheel Mountain King (the path is designated by fifteen kinds of functions).
Thus has been explained the Great Determination of the King of Mountains, the Vajra-Jewel-Wheel.
Next, the Great Determination of the Road of the King of Golden Wheels shall be explained. What are its characteristics? The verse says:
Within the pathways of the King of Mountains, there are fifteen positions in total; for within each of the five types of essential bodies, there are three functions.

Thus the treatise says: Within these pathways of the King of Mountains, the Golden Wheel, how many positions are established as the measure of the pathways? [The following is] the detailed exposition.
Although they are immeasurable, briefly stated there are fifteen kinds of stages (*pada*).
These stages constitute the path-division (*mārga-bhāga*), for as the verse says regarding the path within the King of Mountains, there are fifteen stages in total.
By what causes and conditions are these fifteen fundamental stages clearly understood to exist within this path? It is because of that Vajra-Mahābala-Ratnacakra Mountain.
Because within each of the five types of royal status, there are three distinct modes of sovereign activity, fifteen distinct categories are established based on this principle.
As the verse states: "Within the five types of status, there are three functions each" (Sūtra 15).
Thus, it is said in the *Vaipulya-sūtra*: "The conduct of the king and his subjects within a single district..."
Within each stage (*bhūmi*), there are only fifteen types of essential factors, functions, and numerical positions;

there are no other positions, as explained at length in the citation from the Sūtra (the sixteenth). However, regarding the subtle and wondrous principle, it is stated in the Sūtra that there are twenty-five distinct positions.
This refers to the transition within the royal lineage, not the transition through functional activity. Thus, among the five stages of the Vajra, each position relates to the others...

Possessing five [aspects], they constitute twenty-five distinct stages. Because those that mutually possess [the others] are all the five stages of the fundamental essence, this is called the "transformation of the royal house. Within these divisions, each stage has three functions;

these are the "transformations of activity" (which differ from the aforementioned fundamental stages). How are the names and forms of the fifteen types of stages subsumed under these transformations of activity?
The verse says:
Clarity and distant enumeration, continuity and the three unions, universal movement and universal immobility, the syllables and the extensive,
pervasive arrival and non-pervasive arrival, integration and establishment, and simultaneous detachment—

The treatise says: Within the substance of gradual progression according to sequence, there are three types of function. What are these three?

Because both name and meaning are fully understood, as the verse says, "because of clarity. Second, there is the activity of far-reaching travel and far-reaching cultivation over countless eons;
having passed through these various stages, the accumulation of merit is inexhaustible, as the verse says, "and because of the distant number.
Third, there is the activity of uninterrupted and unceasing constant revolution, occurring moment by moment and in every interval.
It is eternally and constantly uninterrupted because it turns spontaneously. As the verse says, "Because of continuity," this is called the third.
Within the essence of all phenomena (*dharma*), there are likewise three kinds of functions. What are these three? First, the unified function of being able to express and being able to realize;
that is, skillful speech and unimpeded wisdom, which are immeasurable in number because they are a single vajra. Second...

it is the most profound ultimate meaning and the supreme, wondrous, and mysterious principle, which is exclusively one domain and exclusively one body, for there are no two divergent paths. Third is the unification through names according to circumstances;
whatever names may be applied according to their respective contexts, all are entirely the single Golden Body (Suvarṇakāya). These are called the three [unifications]. As it is said:

Because the verse and the [explanation] are combined as three, within the body of the ultimate remainderless state (*nirupadhiśeṣa-niṣṭhā*), there are likewise three kinds of functions. What are these three?

as the verse says, "because it moves everywhere. Second, the pervasive, perfect... [not moving].
Regarding the function of movement: that which thus transforms remains unmoved and unchanging throughout all other infinite states, because it is eternally fixed.
As the verse says, "Because it is universally unmoving. Third, names, phrases, and syllables have no distinct functions;

Pervading the entire body, there are also three kinds of functions. What are these three? First is the function of immeasurable, boundless, and vast activity.
This is because the karmic manifestation of the dharma’s own essence appears as something utterly vast, without any boundaries; as the verse says, "Because it is vast.

Function: All phenomena are entirely eliminated because nothing is asserted; this is as stated in the verse regarding their "dissolution.

As established in the verse: "Third, the dissolution [of the path] wherein both establishment and activity are utterly severed, because it is the ultimate severance of the path and is extensively established.
As the verse says: "Because it is free from both. These are called the three. These are the names of the fifteen stages.
This path and its stages can be thoroughly realized only by those of great faculties; for sentient beings of dull faculties, they are certainly difficult to master.

This concludes [the section]. As the verse says: "These are called the fifteen names; they should be observed in their proper sequence. (The above fifteen types of activity are skillful in expression and profound in meaning.

that is to say, within the fifty-one fundamental great stages,
each and every one is fully established through the five successive stages of gradual transformation.
The Treatise says: Within the essence of this solitary mountain-king, the Mahāśaila-king, how many positions are established as its constituent parts?
Although a detailed explanation would be immeasurable, to state the essentials briefly, there are only one thousand two hundred and seventy-five kinds of definitive positions.
As the verse states regarding the Mahāśaila-king: "In total, within the Mahāśaila-king, there are one thousand two hundred and seventy-five kinds."
Regarding the stages: by what causes and conditions are there one thousand two hundred and seventy-five stages clearly manifested within the essence of the Mountain King?
They are as follows: within the fifty-one kinds of fundamental stages that are eternal and constant, each and every one proceeds through gradual transformation.
All dharmas are thus equal, reaching the ultimate without remainder, universally complete, and simultaneously beyond all negation and detachment—these are the five kinds.

Because they are fully perfected through transformation, and because within each of the five types of stages—such as gradual transformation and so forth—the five distinct sub-stages, beginning with gradual transformation, are individually revealed;

therefore, one thousand two hundred and seventy-five stages are established (the fifty-one fundamental stages, each possessing the five stages such as gradual transformation, constitute two hundred and fifty-five stages.

Furthermore, within each of these five types of stages, such as gradual transformation, there are again the five stages such as gradual transformation, thus resulting in one thousand two hundred and seventy-five stages).

As the verse states, within the fifty-one kinds of the Great Fundamental Stage (*mahāmūlāvasthā*), each and every one is fully established through the five stages, such as gradual transformation and so forth.

Thus, within the essence of this solitary mountain-king, the Mahāśailarāja, these one thousand two hundred and seventy-five kinds of stages likewise transform at each single moment, or transform differently at each single moment. Or...
They all evolve simultaneously; they are also all non-evolving. They evolve at one time in one place; they also evolve at one time in different places;
they also evolve at different times in different places; and they are also all non-evolving. (These eight modes of evolution differ from those in the fourth section.

That section specifically discusses the five stages, whereas this section discusses how each stage mutually contains the others, resulting in one thousand two hundred and seventy-five stages; therefore, the modes of evolution here are further transformed. They are sovereign and spontaneous, unobstructed and unhindered. This is...

Therefore, it is said: "The inexhaustible, vast *dharmadhātu* of the great *tathāgatagarbha*, the fundamental treasury, is the treasury of the Dharma-gates of the ocean of extensive virtues, which are born in each stage (*bhūmi*) without end or limit" (Citation from Scripture, Chapter Seventeen).
Thus it is stated in the *Mahājñānālaṃkāra-dharmadhātu-svabhāva-kāya-gambhīra-sūtra*: "It is beyond comparison or analogy; it is difficult to attain."

It is said: "The treasury within the great ocean and the single essence of the great ocean—within the ground of the original stage, there are three categories of qualities that are fully perfected and without deficiency.
What are these three? First is the category of superior qualities.

Their positions and names are manifold and innumerable, for their measure is equal to the number of atoms in the worlds of the ten directions" (as found in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, regarding the Bhikṣu Sāgaramegha).

One who upholds this "Universal Eye" Dharma-gate: suppose there were a person who, using ink equal in volume to the great ocean and pens as numerous as the Mount Sumerus, were to write down a single gate within one chapter of this sutra, a single dharma within that gate, a single meaning within that dharma, and a single phrase within that meaning—[even with such effort] not even a small fraction could be recorded;
such a person belongs to the category of those with superior virtue. Second is the category of those with middling virtue.

Their rank and names are equal in measure to the number of atoms in hundreds upon hundreds of billions of trichiliocosm worlds; [this is the first category seen by Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna when he entered the Dragon Palace].

The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* [in its supreme version] consists of verses numbering as many as the atoms in thirteen thousand great trichiliocosms and chapters numbering as many as the atoms in one four-continent world system (all of which are subsumed under the category of the supreme class).
Second, the medium-length *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* consists of 498,800 verses and 1,200 chapters (all of which are subsumed under the category of the medium class). Third, the inferior class of categories:

regarding their positions and names, there are 1,275 positions (the inferior-length *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, with 100,000 verses and 48 chapters, is subsumed under the category of the inferior class). These are called the three. As it is said:

These are the various positions. Each and every one of them—indeed, each and every one—is repeated until it reaches the state of immeasurable, immeasurable, immeasurable, immeasurable, immeasurable, immeasurable [times].

(The *cittatathatā-mukha* [Gate of the True Suchness of Mind] is the root of all phenomena; because it is equal and non-dual, it is called "one. There are six stages: Faith, Abiding, Practice, Transference, Grounds, and Buddhahood. These are encompassed by six instances of the character "one.

The *cittapravṛtti-mukha* [Gate of the Arising and Ceasing of Mind] manifests differentiated characteristics and functions that are inexhaustible; these are encompassed by six instances of "immeasurable. (The above four sections constitute the general outline of the Buddha-dharma. The third section elaborates upon the main teaching: it first presents the five stages of the Vajra [nature], which universally encompass the various gateways within the sutras;

it then lists the fifty-one fundamental stages as a basis for reliance. Thus, the ocean of inexhaustible teachings has its main pillars raised and its details displayed. The fourth section summarizes the preceding text and provides a detailed demonstration of the transformative aspects. The fifth section derives fifteen types from within the five stages.)

Its function is the source of boundless wondrous applications. The sixth section, "The Distinctive Features of the Stages," wherein each stage mutually possesses all others, serves as the foundation for the extensive enumeration of dharmas in the subsequent text. The meaning of this entire treatise is revealed with clarity;
that which is called the "Great Fundamental Ground" (Mahābhūmi) is precisely this. The following thirty sections, unfolding in successive layers, all flow forth from within it.

Next, the gate of the distinctions in the meanings and principles expressed shall be explained. Regarding these five kinds of non-empty, determinately abiding phenomena, how many categories does each possess?
This is because each [of these] possesses two kinds. What are the two kinds of freedom from obstruction? First is the freedom from obstruction through maintaining the body;

second is the freedom from obstruction through transformation. Regarding "freedom from obstruction through maintaining the body," it means that the unobstructed body is eternal, constant, and indestructible.
Regarding "freedom from obstruction through transformation," it means establishing all phenomena so as to exercise sovereign mastery over them.

These are called the two [aspects]: guarding the body (which means abiding peacefully and immovably), and transforming (which means responding to conditions without obstruction). What are called the two kinds of substantial existence?
First is the reality of maintaining the body; second is the reality of transformation. Regarding the reality of maintaining the body:

it is because the eternally equal body is constant, perpetual, and never subject to loss or destruction. Regarding the reality of transformation: it is because distinctions are established to bring about stability.
These are called the two. What are the two kinds of the fire of nature? First is the fire that maintains the body...

There are two kinds of fire-nature: first, the fire-nature that maintains the body; second, the fire-nature of transformation. Regarding the fire-nature that maintains the body, it refers to the fact that the body of the treasury of luminous virtue is eternal, constant, and never subject to loss or decay.
Regarding the fire-nature of transformation, it refers to the fact that it transforms together with all sensory objects and conditions, thereby bringing them into accord and fulfillment.
These are called the two. What are the two kinds of present radiance? First is the present radiance of maintaining the body; second is the present radiance of transformation.
As for the present radiance of maintaining the body, it refers to the fact that the body, from its initial blazing forth, is determined to be eternal and constant, never to be lost or destroyed.
As for the present radiance of transformation, it refers to following along with the flow of transmigration without any obstruction. These are called the two.
What are called the two kinds of profundity? First, the profundity of maintaining the body; second, the profundity of transformation.
Regarding the profundity of maintaining the body: it is because one remains detached from the intermediate body, which is eternal, constant, and indestructible.
Regarding the profundity of transformation: it is because one attains mastery over all unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*). These are the two. As previously stated.
Regarding the distinctions in the functional activities of the five kinds of impermanence, what are they respectively? They are as follows:

Because all [defilements] are without remainder; because the destruction of the entire ocean of immeasurable and boundless great merits is without remainder;
and because the obscuration of the mastery over the body—which is neither virtue nor affliction—is without remainder.
One should carefully examine the individual distinctions among the natures and categories of these five dharmas. Thus has been explained the distinction of the meanings expressed.

The Commentary says: What meaning is clarified within this section? It is intended to demonstrate that all fifty-one stages are of equal measure, as they produce a single fruit through two kinds of causes, thereby extensively expanding the ocean of the Three Jewels so that it is inexhaustible. It refers to the two kinds of causes—namely, the cause of faith and the cause of the stage of generating the mind—which possess the same mode of activity and are not distinct from one another.

Next, the two dharmas of the Stage of Mindfulness and the Stage of Joyful Practice are able to nourish the cause; they are fully adorned.
The ocean of the Great Perfect Enlightenment is solemnly adorned; its causal name is "Peaceful Bliss and Eternal Illumination.

It is definitively increasing, free from suffering and delusion, naturally illuminating and penetrating the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*), and constitutes the ocean-like assembly of unobstructed seeds.

Its resultant name is "Eternal Joy and Universal Illumination," the Great Realm of Empty Space. It is profoundly deep, eternally comprehending the non-dual Mountain King. Next is the Ground of Diligence.
The two dharmas of the stage of dedication for the rescue and protection of all sentient beings can nurture the cause, fully adorning the great ocean of a single awakening.
This cause is named the "Emanation of the Water of Supreme Great Compassion Light," which remains far removed from indolence.
Constantly transcending and constantly practicing the fundamental nature of the original ground, one fully masters and penetrates the oceanic assembly of seeds.

The fruit is named the Mountain King of Non-dual Wisdom, which is eternally pervasive through the radiance of compassion. Next, the two dharmas of the Ground of Wisdom-Mind and the Ground of Reversing the Flow of Delight can nurture the cause.

The light of the sun and moon of true vajra; the ocean-like assembly of seed-syllables that is by nature free from suffering and eliminates darkness;

The ocean of awakening is, for this reason, named "Decisive Tranquil Stillness. It is far removed from distraction and illuminates the infinite ocean-assembly of the seeds of water, fire, water, and fire.

Regarding "manifestation of transformation," it refers to the emergence of as many bodies of transformation as there are atoms in a single ten-directional world-system.

Because they enter [the stages] in successive order, these are called the three. Within the context of the transformation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*), each of these likewise possesses these three matters;
one should understand this through extensive application. In this manner, according to each respective stage, all subsequent positions should be understood by analogy with what precedes them.

As the verse begins with "faith" (*śraddhā*), it sequentially leads its own category [of factors] to take up the initial stages of the remaining positions until reaching the stage of "concentrated mind" (*samāhita-citta*), at which point it takes up the stage of the Tathāgata.

Because there are oceans of dharma-gates for each respective causal stage, as numerous as the atoms in the world-systems.

The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is of only one kind; The conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) is of two kinds. Respectively, they are the real and the primordial, and the initial and the subsequent.
The unconditioned is the sovereign; It gives rise to the two kinds of the conditioned. Regarding their progressive increase, vastness, and further development:
The treatise says: The unconditioned is one; the conditioned is two. The first is so called because it possesses reality; The second is so called because it is both primordial and initial.
As the verse says: "The unconditioned has only one; the conditioned has two kinds. This is because, respectively, they are the ultimate reality and the originative and developmental [aspects].

(This is based on the *bhūtakoṭi*: it is said that the unconditioned has only one because it is the single ultimate principle; it is based on conventional truth: it is said that the conditioned has two kinds because the provisional is divided into the originative and the developmental.

Regarding these three dharmas, within the fifty-one stages of the vajra-position, they increase their merits both upward and downward. What is the manner of their transformation? It is said that at the time of ascending:
In each and every stage, the sovereign unconditioned dharmas each give rise to and increase ten thousand fundamental and initial pure, wondrous, and awakened wisdoms.

During the subsequent periods, in each and every stage, two hundred million fundamental and initial pure, wondrous, and awakened wisdoms are fully perfected, given rise to, and increased. In this manner, and so forth, as above.
Down to the smallest *amita* (immeasurable), it is as described in the original text; its retinue is likewise. As the verse says: "The upper and lower lack a master;

they give birth to the two conditioned [realms]. Because they turn toward greater excellence and vastness, one should know that their numerical increase follows this sequence" (*Sūtra-Quotation*, 37).
In the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda-sūtra-śāstra*, within the *Sūtra*, it is stated: "The World-Treasury Ground, the Original King."
Within the ocean of the fundamental source (*mūla-rāja-sāgara*), the qualities of impermanence (*anitya*) are numerous and incalculable, while the qualities of permanence (*nitya*) are extremely few.

For this reason, it is said that the world is like a "treasury-ground" (*loka-kośa-bhūmi*). This is explained at length [in the scriptures]. (The "world as a treasury-ground" is the gate of defilement (*saṃkleśa-mukha*); the "ocean of the fundamental source" is the gate of purity (*vyavadāna-mukha*).
Because defilement has not yet been exhausted and pure karma is not yet perfected, the qualities mostly belong to the impermanent, while the qualities of permanence are exceedingly rare.)

The Twenty-ninth Great Section on the Decisive Determination of the Path of Simultaneous Practice, Unobstructed and Unimpeded, in the Vast Transformation of the Ground of the Spontaneously Arising Sovereign Essence.
Thus has been explained the Great Section on the Decisive Determination of the Chapter on the Great Net of the Spontaneously Arising Sovereign Essence for each of the grounds of bondage.

Next, the section on the Great Determination of the Path that Proceeds with Unobstructed and Unimpeded Purity, which is the Vastly Transforming Stage of the Spontaneous Fundamental King, shall be explained.
What are its characteristics? The verse says:
Within the path of the sovereign fundamental king, it revolves gradually according to its positions.

Because one lord gives rise to two companions, and so on until reaching the infinite within the center, all numerical transformations are universally pervasive. One should observe this in accordance with the Dharma.

The Treatise says: Regarding the stage of the naturally occurring sovereign fundamental king’s vast revolution, it is the section on the path where one proceeds together with non-obstruction and non-hindrance.
In the middle, based on fifty-one stages, one proceeds gradually both upward and downward in successive order.

The unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) acts as the sovereign, giving rise to two conditioned dharmas (*saṃskṛta-dharma*), whether above or below, increasing by immeasurable numbers in the middle until reaching the immeasurable transformations of the middle.
As the verse states: "On the path of the King, proceeding gradually according to the stages, one sovereign gives rise to two companions, until reaching the middle."

Because they are immeasurable, all their numerical transformations are thoroughly pervasive; one should observe them according to the Dharma (Sūtra Citation No. 38). In the *Kusuma-varga* of the *Śākhā-nikāya*, it is stated as follows:
Within the ocean of the treasury of practice (*caryā-kośa-samudra*), there is one quality of permanence, its number being immeasurable.
Within the ocean of the treasury of practice, there are two categories of impermanent qualities, their numbers also being immeasurable; they both ascend and...

[The character 打 (dǎ) is pronounced with the initial *hú* and *yǎ*. Their number is immeasurable. This is explained at length, as follows: (This is the third turning gate. It should correspond to the stage of practice (*caryā-bhūmi*).

Within the ocean of the treasury of practice, it differs greatly from the ocean of the fundamental king of the world-treasury in the preceding section. Therefore, both the constant nature and the non-constant nature are immeasurable; the merit of ascending progress can be seen by reflecting upon this).
Chapter Thirty: The Great Determination of the Ocean of the Inexhaustible Sea of the Mountain King Accompanied by the Most Utterly Vast [Realms].
Thus has been explained the path accompanied by the unobstructed and unhindered state of the vast transformation of the Ground of the Spontaneous Sovereign King.

The Great Section of Determination (*Mahā-viniścaya*). Next, the most extensively vast, co-extensive, mountain-king-like, inexhaustible ocean of oceans, the Great Section of Determination, shall be explained.
What are its characteristics? The verse says:
Within the ocean of the inexhaustible ocean-treasury, one proceeds gradually through the stages;
from one lord producing two companions up to the great immeasurable, the enumeration and transformations follow the previous examples—one should extensively master these.
The Treatise says: Within the inexhaustible ocean-treasury, according to the sequence of the fifty-one stages, it likewise ascends.
Furthermore, it is as follows. The unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*) is the sovereign that gives birth to and increases the two types of conditioned dharmas (*saṃskṛta-dharma*).

It increases them to an immeasurable degree, reaching the state of "greatly immeasurable transformation. As a verse states: "In the midst of an inexhaustible ocean, they evolve gradually according to their stages;

one sovereign produces two companions, until they reach the state of great immeasurability. The numerical and transformative aspects are analogous to what precedes; one should extensively comprehend this. (Citation from the Sūtra, Part Three)
19). In that *sūtra*, it is stated as follows: "Within the ocean of the Constant Mountain King (*nitya-parvatarāja*), there are three kinds of great immeasurables (*mahā-apramāṇa*).
What are the three? First, the constant great immeasurable; second, the impermanent great immeasurable; third, the transformative great immeasurable.

This is explained at length, and so forth. (This is the fourth turning-gate. It should be the stage of dedication (*pariṇāmanā-vasthā*). Dedication toward the sublime fruit is called "practice" [*caryā*].)
The Constant Mountain King. It is eternally concurrent with the impermanent and subject to transformation; all are immensely immeasurable, already designated as the nature of the Dharma-realm.
Chapter Thirty-one: The Great Decision on the Path of Pure Liberation, the Stage of Departing from Bondage.
Thus has been explained the Great Determinative Section on the Inexhaustible Ocean of the Mountain King that Proceeds with the Most Utterly Vast [Qualities].
Next, the Great Determinative Section on the Path of Pure Liberation, the Ground of Deliverance from Bondage, shall be explained.
What are its characteristics? The verse says:
Within the path of liberation, there are twenty unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*), namely the ten emptinesses (*śūnyatā*) and the ten existences (*bhava*).
Such unconditioned phenomena are fully present within the fifty-one stages.
Based on these stages, the turning [of the wheel] is established; therein are two types of "repeated" and "leaping" progressions.
The Treatise says: Within the stage of liberation from bondage (*visaṃyoga-bhūmi*), which is the path of pure and white deliverance, there are twenty unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) eternal dharmas.
These are the ten emptinesses (*śūnyatā*) and the ten existences (*bhava*), each being distinct as unconditioned. (This is the fifth turning gate.

When one suddenly transcends the mundane and supramundane realms while established in the stages, it is called the stage of liberation from bondage; therefore, the ten emptinesses and the ten existences are all unconditioned. As the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "All worthy sages are distinguished by means of the unconditioned dharma.")

This refers to the fact that the fifty-one stages described in this treatise evolve while fully incorporating the twenty varieties of unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) phenomena. What are the ten unconditioned phenomena of emptiness?
First, the unconditioned emptiness of the vast, natural, and eternally abiding empty space that is free from fabrication. Second, the unconditioned emptiness of the shadow of great empty space.
Third, the unconditioned emptiness of the shadow of the shadow of empty space. Fourth, the unconditioned emptiness of the non-existence of the destruction of shadows.

1. The unconditioned of emptiness (*śūnyatāsaṃskṛta*). 2. The unconditioned of the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatāsaṃskṛta*), which is neither [the former] nor empty. 3. The unconditioned of emptiness that transcends speech and is beyond description (*nirabhilāpya-vākpatha-śūnyatāsaṃskṛta*). 4.

The unconditioned of emptiness where transcendence and detachment are not yet complete (*apari-niṣṭhita-viveka-śūnyatāsaṃskṛta*). 5. The unconditioned of emptiness through the liberation of the mind from transcendence and detachment (*citta-viveka-mukti-śūnyatāsaṃskṛta*).

6. The unconditioned of emptiness through the ultimate exhaustion of transcendence and detachment (*atyanta-viveka-kṣaya-śūnyatāsaṃskṛta*). 7. The great emptiness and the great emptiness of emptiness, which are without obstruction and without hindrance (*anāvaraṇa-apratighāta-mahāśūnyatā-mahāśūnyatā-śūnyatāsaṃskṛta*).

These are called the ten. What are the ten unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*)? First, the unconditioned phenomenon that all verbal expressions are definitively, eternally abiding, indestructible, and not empty.
Second, the unconditioned phenomenon that all mental consciousnesses are definitively, eternally abiding, indestructible, and not empty.
Third, the unconditioned phenomenon that all great elements (*mahābhūta*) are definitively, eternally abiding, indestructible, and not empty.
1. All things are neither determinate nor permanent, indestructible, non-empty, and unconditioned. 2. All things are determinate, permanent, indestructible, non-empty, and unconditioned.

3. All things are determinate, permanent, indestructible, non-empty, and unconditioned. 4. All things are entirely neither determinate nor permanent, indestructible, non-empty, and unconditioned. 5. All things possess reality, are determinate, permanent, indestructible, non-empty, and unconditioned.
6. All natures are fire, determinate, permanent, indestructible, non-empty, and unconditioned. 7. All present radiances are determinate, permanent, and indestructible.

1. The indestructible, non-empty, and unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) [nature] of all that is named; 2. The indestructible, non-empty, and unconditioned [nature] of all that is determinately and eternally abiding as named;

3. The indestructible, non-empty, and unconditioned [nature] of all that is nameless; 4. The indestructible, non-empty, and unconditioned [nature] of all that is determinately and eternally abiding as nameless; 5.

The indestructible, non-empty, and unconditioned [nature] of the vast, perfect, and primordially inherent existence of all seeds (sarvabīja); 6. The indestructible, non-empty, and unconditioned [nature] of all that is determinately and eternally abiding as the existence of all seeds.

These are called the ten. As explained in the verse regarding the path of liberation, there are twenty unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*), namely the ten emptinesses (*śūnyatā*) and the ten existences (*bhava*).

Thus, these twenty kinds of unconditioned phenomena function in their full perfection and without deficiency throughout the fifty-one stages of the vajra-position. As the verse states: "Thus all these unconditioned phenomena, within the fifty-one stages..."
Because all are fully present, based on these twenty unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) states, the establishment of the characteristics of transformation across fifty-one stages consists of two types.
What are the two? First, the gate of mutual inclusion without obstruction; second, the gate of sequential, disordered, and transcendent transformation.
These are the two. As the verse says: "Based on the dharmas and the stages, the transformation is established. There is...

Because there is a doublefold, successive transcendence. Furthermore, as for the form and characteristics of the gate of non-obstructive, comprehensive inclusion in its successive layers, the verse says:
"Each of the twenty dharmas Respectively includes the subsequent twenty;
Each of the fifty-one positions Respectively includes all fifty-one positions, And likewise includes those that are their opposites."
For these reasons, the names are established in successive layers.
The treatise asks: What is meant by the characteristic of the gate of successive layers? It means that they are all-encompassing. How are they all-encompassing?
It means that the twenty kinds of unconditioned, eternal dharmas are fully possessed through faith; each one individually encompasses the subsequent stages, with two [dharmas] in each.
Because of the ten kinds of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). As it is said regarding the stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*), so it is for the other stages as well.
Just as the verse states that each of the twenty dharmas individually subsumes the subsequent twenty, so too each of the fifty-one stages individually subsumes fifty-one [stages] without obstruction.
As the verse states: "Each of the fifty-one stages, one by one, subsumes the fifty-one stages. Furthermore...
Each individual dharma encompasses all stages, and each stage encompasses all dharmas, without any obstruction.
This is because, as the verse states, they are mutually inclusive. It is by means of these two types of comprehensive inclusion that the term "repeatedly layered" (*chong-chong*) is established.

As the verse says: "Because of these causes and conditions, the names are established in successive layers. Thus has been explained the gate of non-obstruction through the comprehensive inclusion of successive layers.
Next, the gate of sequential and disordered progression beyond [the stages] shall be explained. What are its characteristics?
The verse says:
Within the fifty-one positions, each undergoes fifty [transformations]; gradually increasing the number of dharmas, they revolve extensively and universally.
The commentary states: What meaning is clarified in this verse? It is intended to demonstrate the fifty-one kinds of vajras.
Within these stages, faith is taken as the first; passing through fifty stages, with the Stage of Resolute Mind (*cittotpāda-vihāra*) as the first;
passing through fifty stages, up to taking the Ultimate Ground (*atyanta-bhūmi*) as the first, passing through fifty stages—if this is the first turning.

In the first turning, there is an increase of four hundred and ten numerical positions. In the second turning, there is an increase of eight hundred and twenty numerical positions, continuing thus until the final stage.
As stated in the verse regarding the fifty-one stages, each successive stage increases by fifty.
"Gradually increasing the number of dharmas, because they turn pervasively and extensively" (Sūtra 40).
In the *Skandha-śaila-rāja-prakāra-sūtra*, within the section on the "Unbreakable Grounds," it is said: "There are many kinds of jewels of tranquility;
there are many kinds of jewels of empty tranquility. If a practitioner enters this gate, they will attain thorough penetration."
All phenomena are the unconditioned Great Way; they are without obstruction and without doubt or fear.
The mind is sovereign, decisively abiding in great peace and bliss. It gradually increases the ocean of constant merit, as explained at length.

(Worldly people know only the treasure of empty stillness, yet do not know that there is also the treasure of quiescence. If there is clamor and movement, it contradicts emptiness. When emptiness and existence contradict one another, this is the dharma of ordinary people and externalists. If one knows that both gates are quiescent, then this is the true, eternal nature and virtue.)
Without admixture and without obstruction).
○ The Thirty-second Great Section on Decisive Selection: The Fundamental Grounds of the Unobstructed Sovereignty of the Mountain King of Liberation.
Thus has been explained the Great Section of Decisive Analysis on the Path of Pure Liberation from the Ground of Deliverance from Bondage.
Next, the Great Section of Decisive Analysis on the Fundamental Grounds of Unimpeded Mastery of the King of Mountains of Liberation shall be explained.
What are its characteristics? The verse says:
Within the Fundamental King of Mountains, emptiness and existence give rise to one another; because all positions arise from one another, they become increasingly superior and expansive.
The commentary states: What meaning is clarified by this verse? It is intended to demonstrate the ten emptinesses of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), each and every one.

Each gives rise to ten unconditioned eternal dharmas. Within these ten unconditioned [dharmas], each one individually gives rise to ten empty unconditioned eternal dharmas (because emptiness gives rise to existence, and existence gives rise to emptiness, it is said that emptiness and existence give rise to one another).

In these fifty-one positions, each one individually gives rise to fifty, because they revolve in a vast and perfect manner through gates such as the "multiple-layered" (*zhongchong*) gate. As stated in the root verse:
Within the King of Mountains, emptiness and existence arise from one another; because all positions arise from one another, they turn toward ever-greater vastness (Sūtra No.
41). Thus it is said in the Mahāyāna-samudra Sūtra: "Within the ocean of liberation, there is both existence and emptiness, and there is also emptiness within emptiness;
these are numerous in number. Such emptiness and existence are exclusively the eternally extinguished (the true, eternal, quiescent extinction)."
It is not of immeasurable quantity; it consists solely of merit and is not of the category of faults (for when a Bodhisattva exhausts this ground, not even the slightest fault can be found).
Therefore, it is called the "Ocean-Treasury of Liberation," as explained at length.
The Thirty-third Great Section on the Great Decision concerning the Great Highway of the King of Mountains of Liberation.
Thus has been explained the Great Section on the Unimpeded Sovereignty of Each Ground in the Fundamental Grounds of the King of Mountains of Liberation.
Next, the Great Path of the Mountain King of Liberation and the Great Section of Decisive Selection shall be explained. What are its characteristics? The verse says:

Within the path of the Mountain King, Amidst the measures previously described, The stages of the "increased emptiness," "emptiness," and "existence" arise, Each succeeding stage being superior to the last.

The Treatise says: Within the section on the Great Highway of the King of Mountains of Liberation, there are three turnings. What are these three? First, the turning of emptiness within emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā-parivarta*):

because each of the ten unconditioned states of emptiness (*daśa-śūnya-asamskṛta*) individually gives rise to ten emptinesses. Second, the turning of existence within existence (*bhāva-bhāva-parivarta*):

because each of the ten unconditioned states of existence (*daśa-bhāva-asamskṛta*) individually gives rise to ten existences. Third, the turning of stage within stage (*avasthā-avasthā-parivarta*): [the five...]

There are eleven stages. Because each and every one gives rise to fifty, these are called the three [categories]. They arise from their own characteristics (*sva-lakṣaṇa*), not from the characteristics of others.

(Emptiness gives rise to emptiness; existence gives rise to existence; stages give rise to stages—all arise from their own characteristics. In the previous section, emptiness and existence were shown to give rise to each other; here, emptiness and existence arise from themselves, which is why they differ.

As stated in the verse regarding the "Road of the Mountain King" (*Girirāja-mārga*) within the previously explained measures: "Emptiness increases through emptiness, existence through existence; at each stage, there arises that which is increasingly superior."
Therefore, one should extensively master the various other gateways, which increase in number through successive stages.
The Thirty-Fourth Section of the Great Determination: The Mountain King of the Vast and Inexhaustible Ocean of Liberation.
Thus has been explained the Great Path of the Great Mountain King of Liberation, the Section on Great Decisive Selection.
Next, the Section on the Great Decisive Selection of the Great Mountain King of the Ocean of Vast and Inexhaustible Liberation will be explained. What are its characteristics? The verse says:
The various transformations previously described are inexhaustible.
The commentary says: What meaning is clarified in this verse? It is intended to demonstrate that the arising of emptiness from itself is inexhaustible;
the arising of emptiness from other emptinesses is inexhaustible; and the arising of emptiness from all existents is inexhaustible. Existents, too...
Thus it is. It is without end. Its stages are likewise without end. Layer upon layer, they are infinite;
revolving in manifold ways, they are infinite. They have no boundary and no beginning or end.

Profoundly profound, universally pervasive, and vast in their unfolding activity, this is because it is the essence, nature, and function of the sovereign, unimpeded King of Mountains within the ocean of liberation (the two gates of emptiness and existence).

It universally encompasses all phenomena of both the mundane and supramundane realms. Through the two gates of successive and simultaneous manifestation, it subsumes all stages, whether sequential or non-sequential. Being without limit, beginning, or end, it comprehensively integrates the three great aspects of essence, attributes, and function.
As for the ultimate, perfectly consummate ocean of fruition, there are no remaining aggregates, because the various transformations previously described in the verses are inexhaustible.
The Thirty-fifth Great Section on the Definitive Selection of the Path of the King of the Treasury of the Great Ocean of Empty Dusts.
Thus has been explained the Great Section on the Definitive Selection of the Great Mountain King of the Ocean of Oceans of Vast and Inexhaustible Liberation.
Next, the Great Determination of the Path of the King of the Ocean-Treasury of the Mahā-śūnyatā-dhūli shall be explained. What are its characteristics?
The verse says:
Within the path of the Ocean King, One is fully endowed with a hundred masteries; For this reason and by these causes and conditions...

Regarding the treatise titled "Establishing the Name of the Ocean King," it says: What meaning is clarified in this verse? It is intended to demonstrate that within the treasury of the Ocean King there is no separate dharma, but only sovereignty.
How many kinds of sovereignty are there? They are of one hundred kinds. What are these one hundred? First:
First is mastery over time (*kāla-vaśitā*). The thirty-two dharmas may transform simultaneously, or they may transform at different times;

they may not transform during the time of transformation, or they may transform during the time of non-transformation; they may transform after a long time, or they may transform after a short time, and so on, up to being immeasurable.
Second is mastery over place (*sthāna-vaśitā*). They may transform in one place or various places, and so on, up to being immeasurable. Third is mastery over things (*vastu-vaśitā*)...

1) Mastery over presence, because it functions as identity, difference, and so forth, up to being immeasurable; 2) mastery over pervasiveness, because there is nothing it does not penetrate, and so forth, up to being immeasurable;

3) mastery over size, because it can be extremely heavy or extremely subtle, and so forth, up to being immeasurable; 4) mastery over existence and non-existence, because it can manifest or remain hidden, and so forth, up to being immeasurable; 5) [Mastery over] manifestation... up to being immeasurable;

6) mastery over transformation, because it transforms all things according to its will, and so forth, up to being immeasurable; 7) mastery over power, because it possesses the power to subdue all beings, and so forth, up to being immeasurable.
7) Mastery over tranquility and movement, because [these] are both concentrated and dispersed, and so forth, up to being immeasurable;

8) mastery over profundity, because [it involves] inconceivable matters and so forth, up to being immeasurable; 9) mastery over non-mastery, because [it involves] contrary matters and so forth, up to being immeasurable;
10) mastery over the unobstructed, because [it involves] contrary and conforming matters and so forth...
Because they reach the immeasurable; even up to the hundredth mastery, such as the mastery of inexhaustibility, all are entirely masterful.
Because they reach the immeasurable, these thirty-two qualities previously mentioned are thus mastered, fully perfected, and proceed without deficiency.
For this reason, he is established with the name "Ocean King. This should be carefully examined and discerned. (From the Third Part)

Having thus explained the thirty-two dharmas, we now explain the hundred kinds of mastery (*vaśitā*) to demonstrate that there is no dharma-gate among the immeasurable ones that does not possess mastery. Ninth is "mastery over non-mastery": even within the most wretched realms of all worlds, there is nothing that is not mastery.

Devadatta, while in the Avīci Hell, experienced it as if he were dwelling in the bliss of the Third Dhyāna Heaven; he was truly one who could realize this path. As stated in the verse from the *Sāgararāja-mārga*:
He is endowed with a hundred masteries (*vaśitā*). For this reason, he is established under the name "Ocean King" (as cited in Sūtra 42).

In the *Buddhāvataṃsaka-sūtra*, within the first extensive section on the "Gates of the Great Ocean," it is stated that if explained in detail, there are as many masteries as there are atoms in a world-system of the ten directions; if explained briefly, there are one hundred masteries. Now...
Because it is explained extensively.
○ The Great Inconceivable, Repeatedly Unfathomable Āśvabhūja Root King,
Great Section of Determination, Chapter Thirty-Six.
Thus has been explained the Great Section on the Decisive Determination of the Path of the King of the Treasury of the Ocean of Great Emptiness.
Next, the Great Section on the Decisive Determination of the Sovereign King of the Inconceivable, Repeatedly Unfathomable, and Inexpressible *Aśvabhava* shall be explained.
What are its characteristics? The verse says:
Within the *Aśvabhū-rāja-sūtra*, there are as many [teachings] as there are atoms in the ten directions, and as many as there are atoms in the emptiness of the ten directions.
The *Triṃśatikā-śāstra* states:
What meaning is clarified in this verse? It is intended to demonstrate that within the ocean of the *Aśvabhū*, all [qualities] are fully present.
The thirty-three oceans of Dharma, as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions;
because they are the thirty-three oceans of Dharma, as numerous as the atoms within the worlds of the ten directions and as numerous as the atoms within the empty spaces of the ten directions.

As stated in the verse from the *Aśvabhūti-rāja-sūtra*: "There are [oceans] as numerous as the atoms of the ten directions, as numerous as the atoms of the emptiness of the ten directions, and thirty..."
Because of the three oceans of dharmas (citing Sūtra 43). In the *Mūla-vastu-sūtra*, it is stated as follows: At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly, saying:
"By means of the three types of supernormal knowledge (*trividyā*), I have thoroughly penetrated all dharmas without obstruction and without deficiency.
Yet there remains one ocean that is inconceivable, utterly inconceivable, and cannot be fathomed—namely..."
The King of the Nature of Emptiness and Dust is the perfect and sovereign treasury of inexhaustible virtues;

thus it is explained at length. (The thirty-three dharmas mentioned above encompass immeasurable dharma-gates and are inexhaustible. The Tathāgata illuminates immeasurable dharmas with immeasurable wisdom; since wisdom is immeasurable, the dharmas are likewise immeasurable.

If one could exhaustively fathom them, they would become finite. Therefore, this section is declared the conclusion of the thirty-four dharmas, just as the *Zhou Yi* concludes with the *Wei Ji* hexagram.)

(Question: Since the twenty-seventh section, the text contains no mention of the names of the stages of faith, abiding, practice, direction, or ground (*śraddhā-vihāra-caryā-pratipatti-bhūmi*). For what reason are these explained by means of the five positions? (Answer: The twenty-seventh section belongs to the stage of bondage (*bandhana-bhūmi*).

It contains the expression "the gate of the first turning," and since wisdom, phenomena, principle, and fruit all pertain to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), how could it not be the stage of faith? In the twenty-eighth section, within the stage of bondage, the Original King appears; there, the two dharmas of the conditioned and the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) turn together.

The impermanent are numerous, while the permanently abiding are few; how could this not be the state of non-abiding? The twenty-nine aspects of permanence and impermanence are all immeasurable in number; furthermore, there is the expression "sailing within the ocean of conditioned phenomena"—how could this not be the state of practice?

Within the thirty divisions, both the permanent and the impermanent, as well as all phenomena of transformation, are immensely vast. Because they are dedicated toward the three locations, they accord with the nature of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). What else could this dedication be? In the thirty-first division, one is liberated from fetters, becoming pure, white, and emancipated.

The ten emptinesses and the ten existences are all unconditioned, eternal dharmas. What else could this be but the stages above the ground (*bhūmi*)? The subsequent four divisions, up to the thirty-fourth, are entirely the characteristics of the Bodhisattva practices on the stages above the ground.

Reaching the thirty-fifth and thirty-sixth divisions, it clarifies that the cause is perfected and the fruit is fulfilled, such that no further dharma can be spoken; it concludes simply by citing the scriptural phrase regarding the "perfection of innate virtues and sovereign mastery. This is what is called the stage of the cause (*hetu-avasthā*) by Xianshou.

This refers to that which can be described as the state of fruition (*phala-avasthā*) yet cannot be fully described.
